eli5.summary: The rules for writing memos about the internet, written as a memo. Newer guides have since replaced it.

questions: request for comments on requests for comments
subtitle: Jon Postel's 1982 memo that tells authors how to state an RFC's purpose and how to format it.

tldr.problem: RFCs came in many kinds, and readers could not always tell whether one was a standard, a discussion or a report. Online copies also had to print on many kinds of equipment.
tldr.mechanism: Each RFC states its intention near the top using one of five sample kinds of paragraph, and follows fixed rules: ASCII, at most 58 lines per page and 72 characters per line.
tldr.outcome: The memo is a specification for RFCs themselves. It was replaced by RFC 1111, RFC 1543 and RFC 2223.

today: RFC 825 has been obsoleted by RFC 1111, RFC 1543 and RFC 2223, so it is no longer the guide for writing RFCs.

sections.title: Purpose of the Memo
sections.content: RFC 825 clarifies the status of RFCs and gives guidance to future authors. It is, in a sense, a specification for RFCs. A memo may be published as an RFC to make information available, to begin or continue a discussion, or to specify a protocol.
sections.eli5: It is a rulebook for how to write the internet's memos, and it explains why anyone would write one.

sections.title: Stating the Intention
sections.content:
Each RFC is to include, on its title page or in the first or second paragraph, a statement describing its intention. The memo offers sample paragraphs for five kinds: Specification (a standard that ARPA Internet hosts are expected to adopt), Discussion (no proposed solutions are standards yet), Information (to solicit reactions), Status (current information, subject to change) and Report (results of a meeting).

The paragraphs need not be copied word for word, but the general intent of the RFC must be made clear.
sections.eli5: Every memo should say right at the top whether it is a rule, an idea to talk about, a news note, a progress update or a meeting report.

sections.title: Format Rules
sections.content:
RFCs are distributed online as public files, and people copy and print them on a wide variety of equipment. To fit, the character codes are ASCII, each page is limited to 58 lines followed by a form feed on a line by itself, and each line is limited to 72 characters followed by carriage return and line feed. Overstriking and underlining are not allowed.

These height and width limits include any headers, footers, page numbers and left indenting.
sections.eli5: Every page has to be the same small size so it prints on any machine, and no fancy underlining is allowed.

sections.title: Distribution and Submission
sections.content: New RFCs are stored as public access files and a short message is sent to the distribution list saying the memo is available. Requests to join or leave the list go to NIC@SRI-NIC, and submissions for RFCs go to POSTEL@USC-ISIF.
sections.eli5: When a new memo is ready, everyone on a mailing list gets a note. To join the list or send in a memo, you write to the addresses given.
